extracted.intended_audience: rulers, princes, statesmen, political advisors, and students of political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidelines for acquiring, securing, and defending principalities (states) — practical standards for rulers on winning followers, handling factions, using cruelty, organizing forces, and avoiding dependence on foreigners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure loyalty by co-opting faction adherents
rubrics_metrics.description: Gain to himself all their adherents who were gentlemen, making them his gentlemen, giving them good pay, and, according to their rank, honouring them with office and command in such a way that in a few months all attachment to the factions was destroyed and turned entirely to the duke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use payment, offices, honour, and patronage to convert members of rival factions into personal supporters; example: the duke weakened the Orsini and Colonnesi by bringing their gentlemen into his service, destroying factional attachment within months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exterminate leaders and turn partisans into friends
rubrics_metrics.description: Having exterminated the leaders, and turned their partisans into his friends, the duke laid sufficiently good foundations to his power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove or neutralize faction leaders and then reconcile/absorb remaining partisans (through mediation, patronage, or rewards) so that the populace comes to accept and appreciate the new order; illustrated by reconciliation at Sinigalia via mediation and bribery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a visible sacrificial punishment to disassociate ruler from necessary cruelties
rubrics_metrics.description: To clear himself in the minds of the people, and gain them entirely to himself, he desired to show that, if any cruelty had been practised, it had not originated with him, but in the natural sternness of the minister. Under this pretence he took Ramiro, and one morning caused him to be executed and left on the piazza at Cesena with the block and a bloody knife at his side. The barbarity of this spectacle caused the people to be at once satisfied and dismayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appoint a harsh enforcer to restore order, then publicly punish or sacrifice that enforcer so the population attributes cruelty to the minister rather than the prince; the spectacle both terrifies and placates the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not depend on foreign powers; seek self-reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Having armed himself in his own way... he had next to consider France, for he knew that the king... would not support him. ... He began to seek new alliances and to temporize with France ... It was his intention to secure himself against them...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While using diplomacy and temporary alliances is prudent, a prince must aim to be independent of foreign armies and influence; build internal strength so foreign withdrawal or hostility does not imperil the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-emptively eliminate dispossessed rivals to remove pretexts for intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: By exterminating the families of those lords whom he had despoiled, so as to take away that pretext from the Pope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove the possibility that dispossessed elites can use external authorities as pretext to reclaim territory; violent removal of rivals is recommended where necessary to secure gains (presented descriptively, with historical example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Win over elite institutions (gentlemen, college) to restrain external authority
rubrics_metrics.description: By winning to himself all the gentlemen of Rome, so as to be able to curb the Pope with their aid... by converting the college more to himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure the loyalty of local elite groups and influential institutions (e.g., college of cardinals) so they act as a domestic bulwark against external interference or hostile successors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid enabling those you have injured to gain high office
rubrics_metrics.description: He ought never to have consented to the election of any cardinal whom he had injured or who had cause to fear him if they became pontiffs. For men injure either from fear or hatred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, prevent persons you have wronged from attaining power that could be used against you; prefer electing those with obligations or friendly ties rather than those who fear or hate you.

rubrics_metrics.name: When seizing a state by wickedness, inflict necessary injuries all at once
rubrics_metrics.description: In seizing a state, the usurper ought to examine closely into all those injuries which it is necessary for him to inflict, and to do them all at one stroke so as not to have to repeat them daily; and thus by not unsettling men he will be able to reassure them, and win them to himself by benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrate necessary cruelties in a single, decisive action to minimize prolonged resentment; follow immediate injuries with gradual benefits so the populace assimilates favors and remains pacified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use severity properly — one decisive application, not continual cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Those may be called properly used... that are applied at one blow and are necessary to one’s security, and that are not persisted in afterwards unless they can be turned to the advantage of the subjects. The badly employed are those which... multiply with time rather than decrease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properly-employed severity is limited, decisive, and followed by mitigation or public benefit; ongoing, repeated cruelty breeds instability and rebellion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live among your people to avoid forced policy changes in crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: A prince ought to live amongst his people in such a way that no unexpected circumstances, whether of good or evil, shall make him change; because if the necessity for this comes in troubled times, you are too late for harsh measures; and mild ones will not help you, for they will be considered as forced from you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistent behavior and policies in peacetime so that policy shifts in crises are not seen as coerced or insincere; this preserves authority and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer popular support over noble support when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: He who obtains sovereignty by the assistance of the nobles maintains himself with more difficulty than he who comes to it by the aid of the people... one cannot by fair dealing, and without injury to others, satisfy the nobles, but you can satisfy the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prince raised by nobles faces powerful equals and conspiracies; a prince with popular support is likelier to have obedient subjects. If elevated by nobles, the prince should strive to win the people by protection and benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make citizens dependent on the state so they remain loyal in adversity
rubrics_metrics.description: A wise prince ought to adopt such a course that his citizens will always in every sort and kind of circumstance have need of the state and of him, and then he will always find them faithful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the populace has material or institutional dependence on the prince/state (employment, security, civic roles) so their self-interest aligns with loyalty, especially in troubled times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure a state's strength by self-sufficiency in military resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who are able to support themselves by their own resources who can, either by abundance of men or money, raise a sufficient army to join battle against any one who comes to attack them... those always to have need of others who cannot show themselves against the enemy in the field, but are forced to defend themselves by sheltering behind walls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a principality can field its own army (men/money). Relying solely on walls or foreign assistance signals weakness and invites cautious aggression unless fortified and well provisioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fortify and provision towns; avoid relying on countryside defense if lacking field army
rubrics_metrics.description: In the second case one can say nothing except to encourage such princes to provision and fortify their towns, and not on any account to defend the country. And whoever shall fortify his town well... will never be attacked without great caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot field forces, invest in strong city defenses, depots (one year's supplies), artillery, and ordinances to deter sieges; focus on urban fortification rather than trying to defend dispersed countryside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public works and employment to keep populace content and ready for defense
rubrics_metrics.description: They also hold military exercises in repute, and moreover have many ordinances to uphold them... they always have the means of giving work to the community in those labours that are the life and strength of the city, and on the pursuit of which the people are supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustain public works, civic employment, and military training to keep the populace economically stable, disciplined, and available for defense — making siege or occupation costly to an attacker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on mercenaries and auxiliaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Mercenaries and auxiliaries are useless and dangerous; and if one holds his state based on these arms, he will stand neither firm nor safe; for they are disunited, ambitious, and without discipline, unfaithful, valiant before friends, cowardly before enemies... they have no other attraction or reason for keeping the field than a trifle of stipend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not build your defense on mercenary forces or auxiliary troops; they are unreliable in war and exploitative in peace. Historical example: the ruin of Italy due to dependence on mercenaries (Charles VIII's ease of conquest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prince should lead in person or rely on citizen-soldiers accountable by law
rubrics_metrics.description: When arms have to be resorted to, either by a prince or a republic, then the prince ought to go in person and perform the duty of a captain; the republic has to send its citizens, and when one is sent who does not turn out satisfactorily, it ought to recall him, and when one is worthy, to hold him by the laws so that he does not leave the command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If war is necessary, the prince must personally command or use citizen-armies with legal structures to appoint, remove, and bind commanders; this produces loyalty and accountability absent in mercenary systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Destroy disloyal soldiery and create new forces loyal to you
rubrics_metrics.description: To destroy a disloyal soldiery and to create new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace untrustworthy troops with forces raised, trained, and remunerated to owe loyalty to the prince, thereby eliminating internal military threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the pragmatic utility (but moral cost) of treachery and calculated wickedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Agathocles... having deliberately resolved to make himself prince and to seize by violence... he assembled the people and the senate of Syracuse... the soldiers killed all the senators and the richest of the people; these dead, he seized and held the princedom... What he achieved cannot be attributed either to fortune or genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machiavelli describes historical examples where deceit, murder, and treachery successfully secured power. The text notes such methods gain empire but not glory — a pragmatic recognition rather than moral endorsement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give benefits gradually to prolong their effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefits ought to be given little by little, so that the flavour of them may last longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After decisive consolidation (including necessary cruelties), distribute rewards, privileges, and reforms incrementally to sustain gratitude and dependency over time rather than exhausting goodwill in a single burst.
